150	An \KWD{extends} clause comes first, if any, and
151	\KWD{excludes},
152	\KWD{comprises},
153	and \KWD{where}
154	clauses come in any order.
155	
156	Each of \KWD{extends}, \KWD{excludes}, and \KWD{comprises} clauses consists
157	of \KWD{extends}, \KWD{excludes}, and \KWD{comprises}
158	respectively followed by a set of trait references
159	separated by commas and enclosed in braces `\txt{\{}' and `\txt{\}}'.
160	If such a clause contains only one trait, the enclosing braces may be elided.
161	In an API (but not a component),
162	a \KWD{comprises} clause may include ``\EXP{\ldots}''.
163	A trait reference listed in the \KWD{comprises} clause is a declared
164	trait identifier (within the same component or an API imported by the
165	component).
166	\note{
167	Victor: Why is this property stated only for a comprises clause?
168	Doesn't it apply to extends and excludes clauses as well?
169	Also, do we really mean ``trait identifier'' above?  Where is that
170	term defined?  Does it include instantiations of parametric traits?}
171	
172	A trait with an \KWD{extends} clause
173	\emph{explicitly extends} those traits listed in its \KWD{extends} clause.
174	\note{
175	Victor: It is possible for a trait to explicitly extend itself
176	 using hidden type variables.  In particular, the straightforward
177	 interpretation of covariant/contravariant declarations has this property.
178	 (But we could just rule this a special case, since it is special in other
179	 ways already.)
180	}
181	\revision{revival-where}{The revival rules on this note and on the
182	one below: a \KWD{where}-clause variable may not appear as a static
183	argument in an \KWD{extends} clause (\secref{where-clauses}),
184	so no trait extends itself through a hidden type variable
185	and explicit extension has no self cycles.}
186	In addition, every trait except \TYP{Any} and \TYP{Object}
187	implicitly extends the trait \TYP{Object}
188	if it does not do so explicitly.
189	We define the extension relation to be the transitive closure
190	of implicit and
191	explicit extension.
192	That is, trait \VAR{T} \emph{extends} trait \VAR{U}
193	if and only if \VAR{T} explicitly or implicitly
194	extends \VAR{U} or if there is some trait \VAR{S}
195	that \VAR{T} explicitly extends and that extends \VAR{U}.
196	The extension relation induced by a program is the smallest
197	relation satisfying these conditions.
198	This relation must form an acyclic hierarchy
199	rooted at trait \TYP{Object}.
200	\note{

200	\note{
201	Victor: Technically, there may be self cycles in explicit extension due to
202	 hidden type variables, as described above.}
203	If a trait \VAR{T} extends trait \VAR{U},
204	or if \VAR{T} and \VAR{U} are the same trait,
205	we say that \VAR{T} is a subtrait of \VAR{U}
206	and that \VAR{U} is a supertrait of \VAR{T}.
207	
208	We say that trait \VAR{T} \emph{strictly extends} trait \VAR{U}
209	if and only if
210	(\emph{i}) \VAR{T} extends \VAR{U} and (\emph{ii}) \VAR{T} is not \VAR{U}.
211	We say that trait \VAR{T} \emph{immediately extends} trait \VAR{U}
212	\note{
213	Victor: I think we don't use ``immediately extends'' anywhere in the spec,
214	  only ``immediate supertype/subtype''.}
215	if and only if (\emph{i}) \VAR{T} strictly extends \VAR{U} and
216	(\emph{ii}) there is no trait \VAR{V}
217	such that \VAR{T} strictly extends \VAR{V}
218	and \VAR{V} strictly extends \VAR{U}.
219	We call \VAR{U} an \emph{immediate supertrait} of \VAR{T}
220	and \VAR{T} an \emph{immediate subtrait} of \VAR{U}.
221	\note{Victor: this belongs in the type chapter.}
222	
223	A trait with an \KWD{excludes} clause excludes
224	every trait listed in its \KWD{excludes} clause.
225	If a trait \VAR{T} excludes a trait \VAR{U},
226	the two traits are mutually exclusive:
227	neither can extend the other, and no trait can extend them both.
228	As discussed in \secref{type-relations},
229	the exclusion relation is symmetric.
230	Thus, if \VAR{T} excludes \VAR{U}
231	then \VAR{U} excludes \VAR{T}
232	whether or not \VAR{T} is listed in an \KWD{excludes} clause
233	in the declaration of \VAR{U}.
234	
235	\note{
236	If a trait declaration of \VAR{T} includes a \KWD{comprises} clause
237	then the traits listed in its \KWD{comprises} clause
238	are exactly the traits that immediately extend \VAR{T}
239	and they must explicitly extend \VAR{T}
240	(i.e., list \VAR{T} in their \KWD{extends} clause).
241	If the \KWD{comprises} clause of a trait \VAR{T} includes ``\EXP{\ldots}''
242	(and must therefore be in an API),
243	then in a component exporting the enclosing API,
244	other traits may explicitly extend \VAR{T},
245	but these traits may not be declared or imported by the API
246	(see \secref{apis}).}
247	
248	
249	For example, the following trait declaration:
250	\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Decl.tex}

253	no static parameters,
254	and

256	no \KWD{comprises} clauses,
257	and no \KWD{where} clauses.
258	Trait \TYP{Catalyst} extends a trait named \TYP{Object}.
259	A single method (named \VAR{catalyze}) is declared, which
260	has a parameter of type
261	\TYP{Reaction} and the return type \TYP{()}.
262	
263	
264	The following example trait:
265	%trait Molecule comprises { OrganicMolecule, InorganicMolecule }
266	%  mass(): Mass
267	%end
268	\begin{Fortress}
269	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Molecule} \KWD{comprises} \{\,\TYP{OrganicMolecule}, \TYP{InorganicMolecule}\,\}\)\\
270	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{mass}()\COLON \TYP{Mass}\)\-\\\poptabs
271	\(\KWD{end}\)
272	\end{Fortress}
273	comprises of two traits: \TYP{OrganicMolecule} and \TYP{InorganicMolecule}.
274	Therefore, the following trait declaration is not allowed:
275	%(* Not allowed! *)
276	%trait ExclusiveMolecule extends Molecule end
277	\begin{Fortress}
278	\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
279	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{ExclusiveMolecule} \KWD{extends} \TYP{Molecule} \KWD{end}\)
280	\end{Fortress}
281	Traits \TYP{OrganicMolecule} and \TYP{InorganicMolecule} may be exclusive:
282	%trait OrganicMolecule extends Molecule excludes InorganicMolecule end
283	%
284	%trait InorganicMolecule extends Molecule end

315	The Working Draft of February 2011 allowed a trait to extend

39	2~February 2011, and only the file \nolinkurl{fortress.1.0.pdf} in it is the
40	Fortress~1.0 release.
41	The full reasoning behind every entry, with each original passage and each
42	new one, is in the revival's decision records,
43	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md}
44	and, for the number chapters,
45	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-numbers/decision-record.md},
46	in the same repository.
47	
48	Every change below follows from one decision of the revival, taken on
49	24~September 2026 and called \emph{route~A}: the compiled type checker keeps
50	the type group's rule that no type is a subtype of two different
51	instantiations of one parameterized trait, a rule this working draft never
52	stated, and the library's numeric types are reorganized so that they
53	satisfy it.
54	The revision of the number chapters (\secref{revival-numbers} to
55	\secref{revival-reductions}) also carries out three decisions of
56	26~September 2026 that follow from route~A: on the refined number types, on
57	conversions between number types, and on sums and products.
58	The alternative not taken, \emph{route~C}, is described once, in
59	\secref{revival-routec}.
60	
61	\subsection{Instantiation exclusion}
62	\seclabel{revival-rule}
63	
64	\begin{description}
65	\item[Affected sections] \secref{trait-types}; \secref{trait-decls}.
66	\item[Change] A property of the exclusion relation is added:
67	two instantiations of the same parameterized trait exclude each other
68	unless every static argument other than an operator argument is the same.
69	The rule it imposes on declarations is added beside the example of
70	\TYP{InclusiveMolecule}: a trait or object may not extend two such
71	instantiations, directly or through its supertraits.
72	\item[Rationale] Without the rule a value may belong to two instantiations
73	of one parameterized trait, and code specialised for one of them can be
74	chosen for a caller that was promised the other; with the rule relaxed, the
75	compiled implementation accepts such a program and fails at run time.
76	The type group adopted the rule as \emph{multiple instantiation exclusion}
77	(Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type
78	Checking Modular Multiple Dispatch with Parametric Polymorphism and
79	Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011), and the compiled type checker has
80	enforced it since 2010.
81	The team's later, unfinished Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) states it in
82	the two parts used here, under the name \emph{instantiation exclusion}.
83	Operator arguments do not count: an operator argument only names the
84	operator a subtrait inherits (\secref{opr-ident}), neither implementation
85	distinguishes instantiations by it at run time, and the algebra of the
86	library chapters depends on types that are several instantiations of one
87	trait differing only in operator arguments.
88	\KWD{nat}, \KWD{int} and \KWD{bool} arguments count: they are values at
89	run time (\secref{natparams}, \secref{boolparams}).
90	\item[Effect] Programs in which a type is a subtype of two instantiations
91	of one parameterized trait that differ in any other static argument are no
92	longer valid. The compiled type checker refuses them where the arguments
93	that differ are types, or numerals given as \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int}
94	arguments (row~402 of the revival's gap ledger). It does not yet refuse
95	them where those arguments are \KWD{bool} arguments, though it accepts boolean parameters written out (row~406),
96	or where one of them is a static parameter of the trait or object that extends both (row~414).
97	The interpreter does not check the rule.
98	The number chapters are revised to the reorganized numeric types
99	(\secref{revival-numbers}).
100	\item[Original text] The Working Draft of February 2011 states no such
101	property; its relations are ``the smallest ones that satisfy all the
102	properties given in those sections (and this one)''
103	(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex}, lines
104	185--189), and the properties it gives for trait types are these (lines
105	212--216):
106	\begin{quote}
107	A trait declaration may also include an \KWD{excludes} clause,
108	in which case the defined trait type
109	excludes every type that appears in that clause.
110	Every trait type also excludes every arrow type and every tuple type,
111	and the special types \TYP{()} and \TYP{BottomType}.
112	\end{quote}
113	Its rule on declarations is only that of exclusive traits,
114	``no trait can extend them both''
115	(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, lines 218--222).
116	\item[Route C] Replaces this rule by the rule of \secref{revival-routec}.
117	\end{description}
118	
119	\subsection{Where-clause variables in extends clauses}
120	\seclabel{revival-where}

1071	\subsection{The integer type of a range}
1072	\seclabel{revival-ranges}
1073	
1074	\begin{description}
1075	\item[Affected sections] \secref{ranges}; \secref{basic-integers};
1076	\secref{revival-numbers}; \secref{revival-notrevised}.
1077	\item[Change] The components of an explicit range are values of type
1078	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, into which an integer numeral converts, and it is a static
1079	error if a component has another integer type. A paragraph shows how a loop
1080	whose counter must have a wider integer type is written: over a range of
1081	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} values, widening each element.
1082	The box in \secref{basic-integers}, the effect of \secref{revival-numbers} and
1083	\secref{revival-notrevised} no longer say that a range over two different
1084	integer types infers the narrowest type that both coerce into; they keep that
1085	rule for a generic call.
1086	\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
1087	it on 27~September 2026.
1088	The Working Draft named no integer type for a range, and \library\ declared
1089	their ranges generic over an integer type named by a type parameter. The
1090	compiled type checker refused that code wherever it converted a numeral to the
1091	range's integer type, since a numeral does not convert to a type named by a
1092	type parameter (\secref{using-coercion}).
1093	The compiled path's own smaller library declares its ranges over
1094	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} alone (\nolinkurl{Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi}, lines
1095	173--174), and on the Java Virtual Machine, which runs Fortress, an array holds
1096	at most $2^{31}-1$ elements, so a range of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} values indexes any
1097	of them.
1098	With every range over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, no range is over two different
1099	integer types, and the rule that infers the narrowest type that both coerce
1100	into concerns a generic call alone.
1101	The full reasoning is in
1102	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-ranges/decision-record.md}
1103	in the revival's repository.

1105	one over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} or
1106	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, and widens its elements where it needs a wider counter; a
1107	range over another integer type is refused. Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter may
1108	be a component of a range is not settled (\secref{revival-notrevised}).
1109	\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/ranges.tex},

1119	61--65, before this revision:

1143	\subsection{Examples and a property with ranges over wider integer types}
1144	\seclabel{revival-range-examples}

1148	\figref{generatorDefn} and the generator adapted to a commutative monoid;
1149	\secref{basic-integers}.
1150	\item[Change] The function \VAR{mySum} of \secref{block-expr} takes a parameter
1151	of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and keeps its sum of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}.
1152	The generator of \figref{generatorDefn}, and the generator of
1153	\secref{defining-generators} that adapts it to a commutative monoid, are
1154	declared over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and the figure's midpoint is
1155	\EXP{\VAR{lo} + (\VAR{hi} - \VAR{lo}) \div 2}.
1156	The factorial property of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} is stated by the value at \EXP{0} and
1157	a recurrence, without a range.
1158	\item[Rationale] Each built a range over an integer type other than
1159	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\secref{revival-ranges}): the loop of \VAR{mySum} over
1160	\EXP{0\COLONOP{}i} with \VAR{i} of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, the method
1161	\VAR{seq} of the figure's generator over \EXP{\VAR{lo}\COLONOP\VAR{hi}} with
1162	bounds of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, and the property's product over
1163	\EXP{1\COLONOP{}m} with \VAR{m} of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}. The adapted generator
1164	builds no range in its own text, but its ellipsis stands for the figure's
1165	members.
1166	The figure's midpoint \EXP{\left\lfloor (\VAR{lo}+\VAR{hi})/2 \right\rfloor} is a
1167	value of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (\secref{basic-rationals}), which converts to
1168	neither \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} nor \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\secref{basic-integers}), so
1169	the recursive construction of the generator did not accept it; the new
1170	midpoint is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} value equal to it whenever \EXP{\VAR{lo} \leq \VAR{hi}}
1171	and the generator's size \EXP{\VAR{hi}-\VAR{lo}+1} is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} value, and
1172	it does not form the sum \EXP{\VAR{lo}+\VAR{hi}}, which exceeds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}
1173	when both bounds are large.
1174	The property of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} holds for every natural \VAR{m}; over a range
1175	of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} values it would hold only below $2^{31}$ and need two
1176	conversions, so it is stated by a recurrence, as \secref{basic-integers} states
1177	the binomial coefficient by Pascal's rule.
1178	\item[Effect] None beyond the examples and the property.
1179	\item[Original text] The two examples are typeset from the files
1180	\nolinkurl{SpecData/examples/basic/Expr.Do.mySum.fss} and
1181	\nolinkurl{SpecData/examples/advanced/Generators.GeneratorDefn.fss} of the
1182	revival's repository, identical in the commit of 2~February 2011 of which
1183	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/} is a copy and unchanged until this
1184	revision;
1185	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/blocks.tex}, line 72,

1188	\begin{quote}
1189	\begin{FortressCode}
1190	\VAR{mySum}(i\COLON\mathbb{Z}64)\COLON\mathbb{Z}64 =\; \KWD{do} \\
1191	\2\+\VAR{acc}\COLON\mathbb{Z}64 \ASSIGN 0 \\

1194	  \KWD{end} \\
1195	  \VAR{acc}\- \\
1196	\KWD{end}
1197	\end{FortressCode}
1198	\end{quote}
1199	and
1200	\begin{quote}
1201	\begin{FortressCode}
1202	\KWD{object} \TYP{BlockedRange}(\VAR{lo}\COLON \mathbb{Z}64, \VAR{hi}\COLON \mathbb{Z}64, b\COLON \mathbb{Z}64) \KWD{extends} \TYP{Generator}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket \\

1243	\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
1244	\end{description}
1245	
1246	\subsection{Passages not yet revised}
1247	\seclabel{revival-notrevised}
1248	
1249	No passage that instantiation exclusion or the reorganized numeric types
1250	contradict is known to be unrevised.
1251	The rule by which a generic call over two different integer types
1252	infers the narrowest type that both coerce into is to be written into
1253	\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation
1254	(\secref{revival-numbers}). The result of an integer raised to a negative power is not yet given (\secref{basic-integers}; \secref{revival-integers}).
1255	Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter, which may appear wherever a variable of type
1256	\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can (\secref{natparams}), may be a component of a range
1257	is not settled (\secref{revival-ranges}); the static ranges of
1258	\secref{ranges} and the examples whose ranges a \KWD{nat} parameter bounds are
1259	not revised.
1260	Before the number chapters were revised, this section said:
1261	\begin{quote}
1262	The number chapters, \chapref{lib:numbers-basic} (whose integers are \secref{basic-integers})
1263	and \chapref{lib:numbers-advanced}, are not yet revised.
1264	Their nested tower, in which each integer type is a subtype of the rational
1265	one above it and each carries its algebra at its own type, and the
1266	conditional self-extension of \TYP{RationalQuantity}, are refused by
1267	instantiation exclusion, as the compiled type checker refuses the
1268	library's nested tower today.
1269	They will be revised together with the reorganization of the library's
1270	numeric types that route~A decides, and not before, because a
1271	specification ahead of its library is as much an open discrepancy as one
1272	behind it.
1273	Until then the rule refuses the tower these chapters describe.
1274	\end{quote}
1275	
1276	\subsection{Route C, the alternative not taken}
1277	\seclabel{revival-routec}
1278	
1279	The team's 2012 patent applications (US~8,843,887 and US~8,898,632;
1280	Chase, Steele, Naden, Hilburn, and Luchangco) relax the rule for a
1281	self-typed parameterized trait: a type may be a subtype of several of its
1282	instantiations when they form a chain.
1283	The revival built that rule whole as an experiment and measured it.
1284	It closes the unsoundness that instantiation exclusion guards against only
1285	together with a rule on return types over every level of a chain and a
1286	change in how a call chooses among generic methods specialised to
1287	different instantiations: 188 lines of code in five files of the compiled
1288	type checker and code generator.
1289	Reversing route~A for route~C would also need a method per level of a
1290	chain in the code generator, work in the interpreter, a way past a stack
1291	overflow of the type checker on the self-typing clauses, and seven library
1292	declarations, besides undoing the reorganization of the library's numeric
1293	types.
1294	Route~C rescues none of the \KWD{where}-clause examples of
1295	\secref{where-clauses} nor the \TYP{Nothing} of \secref{convenience-types},
1296	each of which places one type below infinitely many instantiations, which
1297	no chain contains.
1298	Under route~C the numeric chapters could have kept the nesting of their
1299	widths, and their original text, quoted in \secref{revival-numbers} and the
1300	entries after it and kept in the Working Draft of February 2011, is route~C's
1301	for that nesting; route~C rescues neither the refined number types nor
1302	\TYP{RationalQuantity} (\secref{revival-numbers}).
1303	The record of the experiment is
1304	\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md} in the
1305	revival's repository.
1306	\fussy

356	% which defines the exclusion relation for different instantiations of a generic type:
357	Two instantiations of a generic trait type exclude each other 
358	if the corresponding arguments for any covariant parameter exclude each other, 
359	or if the corresponding arguments for any non-covariant parameter 
360	are not type equivalent.
361	\note{I believe this exactly characterizes exclusion
362	among different instantiations of a generic type, 
363	but the rule we impose is stronger:
364	Any trait that extends (possibly indirectly) 
365	two instantiations of a generic type 
366	must extend an \emph{expressible} instantiation of that generic type 
367	that is a subtype of both.
368	In other words,
369	among all instantiations of a generic type 
370	that are supertypes of some expressible trait type, 
371	one must be a subtype of all the others, 
372	and it must be expressible.
373	This section should say only which instantiations exclude each other,
374	as it does.
375	It perhaps should make it clearer that what is said here 
376	is a consequence of instantiation exclusion, 
377	which is a rule applied to trait declarations.}
378	
379	
380	% An object trait type is a leaf type:
381	An object trait type has no strict subtype other than \Bottom, 
382	and it excludes any type that is not its supertype.
383	
384	A trait declaration may have a \KWD{comprises} clause, 
385	which also specifies a set of types and 
386	generic types determined by the generic type of the declaration.
387	An instantiation of the generic type defined by such a declaration 
388	is covered by the union 
389	of the types in this set 
390	and the corresponding instantiations of the generic type in this set.
391	
392	% Victor: I'm not sure about the proper terminology here.
393	A trait or object declaration may provide a \emph{coercion} from a type or a generic type.
394	(See \secref{coercion-decl} and \chapref{coercion}.)
395	If a trait or object declaration provides a coercion from a type, 
396	then any instantiation of the generic type defined by that declaration 
397	coerces that type.
398	If it provides a coercion from a generic type, 
399	then an instantiation of the generic type defined by that declaration 
400	coerces the corresponding instantiation of the generic type of the coercion.
